80561.title: Incorrect S3 metadata path resolution when config is populated in Iceberg REST catalog /v1/config response
80561.feasibility_reason: The issue provides a clear description of the problem where ClickHouse's S3 metadata path normalization fails when an s3.endpoint config is returned by the Iceberg REST catalog /v1/config response. However, fixing this requires understanding ClickHouse's internal Iceberg REST catalog client and path resolution logic, which may touch complex storage or datalake integration subsystems.
80561.problem_summary: When an Iceberg REST catalog returns an 's3.endpoint' config (e.g., pointing to MinIO), ClickHouse fails to recognize matching prefixes between data_location and metadata_location due to URI scheme/host differences. This causes the entire metadata_location to be appended to data_location, yielding an invalid object storage key with an embedded URI.
80561.root_cause_hypothesis: ClickHouse resolves relative Iceberg metadata paths using a naive string prefix check (`metadata_location.starts_with(data_location)`). When 's3.endpoint' is configured, data_location may be constructed with the HTTP/S endpoint prefix or normalized endpoint URL, while metadata_location retains an 's3://' scheme (or vice versa). Because string prefixes differ, the prefix is not stripped and metadata_location is treated as a relative path to data_location.
80561.suggested_approach: Normalize both data_location and metadata_location into standardized object storage paths (e.g., stripping URI schemes like 's3://', 'http://', 'https://' and endpoint hostnames/bucket names or parsing them into consistent bucket and key components) prior to calculating relative paths, or parse metadata_location using the object storage URI parser to extract the relative key directly.
prerequisites: Local ClickHouse build environment with S3 and Iceberg integration enabled
Docker environment to spin up MinIO and an Iceberg REST catalog (e.g. Apache Lakekeeper or Nessie) for reproduction and integration testing
implementation_steps: Locate the path resolution snippet where `metadata_location.starts_with(data_location)` is evaluated (likely within the Iceberg catalog or metadata handling code in `src/Storages/DataLakes/Iceberg/` or `src/Databases/DataLakes/`)
Analyze how `data_location` and `metadata_location` are constructed when 's3.endpoint' is parsed from the Iceberg REST `/v1/config` response

Implement URL/path normalization using ClickHouse's S3/URI utilities (e.g., `S3::URI`) to extract bucket and object key from both URLs regardless of whether scheme is `s3://`, `http://`, or `https://`
Update the prefix comparison logic to operate on the normalized key path or bucket/key pairs instead of raw strings
Add unit tests for path normalization covering `s3://` URLs against custom endpoints (`http://minio:9000/<bucket>/<path>`)
Add or update integration tests with MinIO and Iceberg REST catalog verifying that metadata and table contents can be queried without path duplication errors

76518.title: INSERT SELECT fails during schema inferece if the same identifier is used in projection list
76518.feasibility_reason: The issue involves schema inference during an INSERT SELECT statement where duplicate projected identifiers or expressions cause column collision errors. While reproducible with a clear example, understanding where schema inference builds the columns list for INSERT SELECT requires navigating the query execution and table block structures.
76518.problem_summary: INSERT SELECT queries against table functions (such as s3Cluster or s3) fail with ILLEGAL_COLUMN (column with this name already exists) during query analysis and schema inference when the same column identifier is projected multiple times in the SELECT clause.
76518.root_cause_hypothesis: During query analysis of table functions in QueryAnalyzer::resolveTableFunction, schema inference inspects the SELECT projection list to determine the requested columns. When the same underlying column (e.g., `size`) is referenced multiple times with different aliases, its name is added repeatedly to a ColumnsDescription collection without deduplication or checking whether the column has already been added.
76518.suggested_approach: Deduplicate requested column names or check whether a column already exists in ColumnsDescription using `has()` before invoking `ColumnsDescription::add()` during table function schema inference and query analysis.
prerequisites: C++20 development environment configured for ClickHouse
Ability to build and run ClickHouse analyzer tests
implementation_steps: Locate the column extraction logic inside `QueryAnalyzer::resolveTableFunction` in `src/Analyzer/QueryAnalyzer.cpp`.
Identify the loop or helper function where column names from query tree nodes are added into the `ColumnsDescription` structure for schema inference.
Update the logic to deduplicate column names or check `columns_description.has(column_name)` before calling `columns_description.add(...)`.
Add functional SQL tests in `tests/queries/0_stateless/` reproducing `INSERT INTO ... SELECT col AS x, col AS y FROM s3Cluster(...)` to prevent regressions.

58479.title: Query with broken link cannot be cancelled while reading from S3
58479.feasibility_reason: The issue identifies a specific place where cancellation checks are missing during S3 read retries, but diagnosing network timeouts and integrating cancellation tokens into the third-party or internal S3 client retry loop can be tricky without breaking error handling.
blockers: Cancellation token propagation in network client loops
58479.problem_summary: Queries querying broken or unresponsive S3 links hang during connection/retry attempts and cannot be cancelled or aborted via timeouts.
58479.root_cause_hypothesis: S3 reading and retry loops (e.g. in ReadBufferFromS3, S3 request retry callbacks, or S3 client initialization) execute blocking network calls synchronously without inspecting Context::checkTimeLimit() or query cancellation tokens between retry attempts.
58479.suggested_approach: Inject query cancellation checks into the S3 retry loops and ReadBufferFromS3 read/initialization paths, ensuring that when the client sends a cancel packet or when query timeouts expire, the S3 retry loop breaks immediately and raises an execution cancellation exception.
prerequisites: Ability to run and build ClickHouse with S3 storage support enabled
Understanding of ClickHouse query execution context, cancellation mechanisms (e.g., QueryStatus, isCancelled, checkTimeLimit), and AWS SDK / S3 retry mechanisms
implementation_steps: Identify where S3 requests are retried and where blocking connections are initiated during S3 read buffer creation (such as ReadBufferFromS3 and S3 client request handlers).
Expose or pass the query execution Context or its QueryStatus / cancellation token into the S3 reading buffers and retry strategy callbacks.
Hook into the retry callback / sleep interval before retrying S3 HTTP requests to verify whether the query has been cancelled or timed out (via isCancelled() or checkTimeLimit()).
If cancelled, interrupt retry sleeping, abort in-flight requests if possible, and throw an exception (e.g., DB::Exception with ErrorCodes::QUERY_WAS_CANCELLED).
Ensure S3Source or async pipeline reader handles the cancellation error gracefully and propagates the cancellation status to the query execution pipeline.

Add integration or unit tests simulating an unreachable S3 endpoint to verify that cancelling the query (Ctrl+C / client cancel packet) terminates the query quickly instead of waiting for full retry timeouts.

58928.title: `kafka_skip_broken_messages` is silently ignored for `Protobuf` and `ProtobufSingle` formats
58928.feasibility_reason: The issue clearly identifies a bug where kafka_skip_broken_messages is ignored specifically for Protobuf formats in the Kafka table engine. Fixing it requires understanding how format-specific error handling interacts with the Kafka streaming reader, but it is localized to the integration between Kafka engine and the Protobuf parser.
58928.problem_summary: The `kafka_skip_broken_messages` setting is ignored when using `Protobuf` or `ProtobufSingle` formats in Kafka tables, causing queries or stream processing to throw exceptions on invalid message payloads rather than skipping them up to the set budget.
58928.root_cause_hypothesis: Exceptions thrown during Protobuf message header or payload parsing (such as length-varint decoding or field parsing in `ProtobufRowInputFormat`) bypass the broken message handling logic in `StorageKafka` or are not properly isolated per Kafka message, causing execution to terminate prematurely.
58928.suggested_approach: Audit exception propagation and input stream reset behavior in `StorageKafka` and `ProtobufRowInputFormat`. Ensure message boundary parsing failures in Protobuf formats are caught by the Kafka engine input handling loop so that broken messages increment the skipped message counter and allow consumption of subsequent valid messages.
prerequisites: Ability to build ClickHouse from source with Kafka component support.
Local test environment with integration test setup using Kafka (e.g. runner or docker-compose integration tests).
implementation_steps: Trace `StorageKafka` message reading loop to verify how broken message exceptions are handled across different format types.
Analyze `ProtobufRowInputFormat` and `ProtobufSingleRowInputFormat` exception locations during varint length parsing and protobuf deserialization.
Ensure parsing errors inside a single Kafka message trigger the `kafka_skip_broken_messages` fallback in `StorageKafka` without corrupting the stream state for subsequent Kafka messages.

Add or update integration tests in `tests/integration/` verifying that malformed Protobuf and ProtobufSingle messages are skipped up to `kafka_skip_broken_messages` while valid messages are correctly inserted.

87575.title: Lazy materialization: Method deserializeBinaryBulk of SerializationAggregateFunction does not support cases where rows_offset {} is non-zero
87575.feasibility_reason: The issue provides a clear error message, stack trace context, and reproduction schema, but implementing deserializeBinaryBulk with a non-zero rows_offset in SerializationAggregateFunction requires understanding the binary bulk deserialization protocol and how lazy materialization handles offsets for aggregate functions.
87575.problem_summary: Queries on AggregateFunction columns fail with NOT_IMPLEMENTED when lazy materialization reads data starting at a non-zero row offset within a granule.
87575.root_cause_hypothesis: `SerializationAggregateFunction::deserializeBinaryBulk` does not implement support for non-zero `rows_offset`, throwing `DB::Exception(ErrorCodes::NOT_IMPLEMENTED, ...)` when lazy materialization attempts to read rows starting at an offset within a mark.
87575.suggested_approach: Implement handling for `rows_offset > 0` in `SerializationAggregateFunction::deserializeBinaryBulk` (and `deserializeBinaryBulkWithMultipleStreams` if applicable) by deserializing and discarding `rows_offset` elements from the stream before deserializing `limit` rows into the destination column, or by skipping serialized states appropriately.
prerequisites: C++20 development environment configured for ClickHouse build
Understanding of ClickHouse columnar serialization (`ISerialization`, `deserializeBinaryBulk`) and AggregateFunction state deserialization
Understanding of lazy materialization reader mechanics and offsets in marks
implementation_steps: Locate `SerializationAggregateFunction::deserializeBinaryBulk` in `src/DataTypes/Serializations/SerializationAggregateFunction.cpp`.
Examine how other `ISerialization` implementations handle non-zero `rows_offset` when deserializing bulk streams.

Update `SerializationAggregateFunction::deserializeBinaryBulk` so that when `rows_offset > 0`, it allocates a temporary AggregateFunction state (or uses temporary memory) and deserializes/destroys `rows_offset` items to advance the read stream.

Ensure `deserializeBinaryBulkWithMultipleStreams` or any relevant stream reading helpers in `SerializationAggregateFunction` properly propagate and handle `rows_offset` without throwing `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`.

58662.title: Support defaults in Native format
58662.feasibility_reason: The issue requests adding a new data format 'NativeWithDefaults' similar to an existing 'RowBinaryWithDefaults' format. While the pattern exists elsewhere in the codebase, implementing a new format in ClickHouse involves deep C++ knowledge of serialization/deserialization routines, block processing, and format registries.
blockers: Requires understanding the complex ClickHouse block input/output and format serialization internals.
58662.problem_summary: ClickHouse's Native format currently requires all column values to be provided explicitly on the client side, making it impossible to let the server evaluate default expressions during insertion in Native format.
58662.root_cause_hypothesis: The Native input format strictly deserializes blocks containing full columns matching the provided structure and does not provide a mechanism to fill in omitted columns using server-side default expressions, unlike formats like RowBinaryWithDefaults.
58662.suggested_approach: Implement a new format 'NativeWithDefaults' (modeled after RowBinaryWithDefaults) by creating or adapting Native format processors that read incoming Native blocks with a subset of columns and evaluate server-side defaults for any missing columns based on table metadata.
prerequisites: Familiarity with ClickHouse's Native block serialization format
Understanding of ClickHouse IInputFormat / IOutputFormat processors and FormatFactory registration
Review of PR/issue #50854 (RowBinaryWithDefaults) for the defaults evaluation pattern via evaluateMissingDefaults
implementation_steps: Review the implementation of RowBinaryWithDefaultsBlockInputFormat and how it utilizes ActionsDAG / evaluateMissingDefaults to populate missing columns.
Add format registration for 'NativeWithDefaults' in FormatFactory (with appropriate FormatSettings flags or dedicated input/output format classes).

Implement NativeWithDefaultsBlockInputFormat inheriting from or wrapping NativeBlockInputFormat, modifying block reading so that columns missing in the input stream are generated and filled according to table default expressions.
Ensure NativeWithDefaults handles cases where block column headers differ from the expected schema by filling missing columns and correctly ignoring/reordering columns if needed.
Optionally implement NativeWithDefaultsBlockOutputFormat if output behavior needs to distinguish default handling, or alias it to standard Native output format.
Write comprehensive stateless tests in tests/queries/0_stateless to verify inserting tables with default, materialized, and alias columns using FORMAT NativeWithDefaults.
Add documentation for NativeWithDefaults format under docs/en/interfaces/formats/.

65251.title: Replicated database: Stuck DDL after a failed DROP DATABASE
65251.feasibility_reason: The issue involves a specific filesystem error during a DROP DATABASE due to extremely long file names when moving to metadata_dropped, which leaves the replicated database in a stuck DDL/ZooKeeper state. While the reproduction steps are clear, dealing with replicated database DDL queues and filesystem path length limits requires careful handling.
65251.problem_summary: Dropping a Replicated database containing a table with a long name fails with ENAMETOOLONG when ClickHouse renames metadata files into `metadata_dropped/`. This leaves the database's DDL worker stopped (`stop_flag = true`), rendering the database unusable and freezing the DDL queue even across restarts.
65251.root_cause_hypothesis: When moving metadata files of dropped tables to the `metadata_dropped/` directory, ClickHouse constructs a filename combining database name, table name, and UUID (`<db>.<table_name>.<uuid>.sql`). When the combined length exceeds the filesystem's `NAME_MAX` (typically 255 bytes), `std::filesystem::rename` throws an exception. In `DatabaseReplicated`, the drop database logic stops the DDL worker and sets `stop_flag = true` before/during execution, but does not recover or restart the DDL worker if dropping metadata or tables throws an unhandled exception.
65251.suggested_approach:
1. Ensure filename lengths destined for `metadata_dropped/` never exceed `NAME_MAX` (255 bytes) by truncating the prefix or hashing excess characters while keeping the UUID and `.sql` suffix unique.
2. In `DatabaseReplicated`, ensure proper exception safety during database drop / DDL queue execution so that the DDL worker is not left permanently stopped on failure or that failures can be properly unwound/reported without bricking the queue.
prerequisites: A local ClickHouse build environment with Keeper / ZooKeeper enabled for integration testing
Understanding of ClickHouse `DatabaseCatalog` metadata management and `DatabaseReplicated` DDL queue processing
implementation_steps: Inspect the logic responsible for creating filenames in `metadata_dropped/` (typically in `DatabaseCatalog::removeTableFromCatalog` or `DatabaseOnDisk`).

Implement filename length sanitization for `metadata_dropped/`: if the constructed filename exceeds `NAME_MAX` (or 255 bytes), truncate the `database.table` component or replace the overflow with a hash while preserving the UUID and `.sql` extension.

Examine `DatabaseReplicated::dropDatabase` and `DDLWorker` execution: wrap the drop/removal operations so that if an unhandled exception occurs during drop execution, the DDL worker state / `stop_flag` is either restored or cleaned up safely instead of wedging the replication queue.

Verify behavior during DDL task execution: check why the DDL task gets stuck retrying indefinitely on unrecoverable filesystem errors, and verify if existing error-handling mechanisms (like marking the DDL task failed in Keeper) apply.
Add functional tests with long table names in a Replicated database verifying that `DROP DATABASE` succeeds without filesystem errors and does not stall subsequent DDL queries.

71793.title: Deletion Error with Ephemeral Column in Table
71793.feasibility_reason: The issue involves mutations in ClickHouse failing when ephemeral columns are present due to missing column resolution during mutation planning. While reproducible, it requires understanding ClickHouse's internal mutation and storage subsystems.
blockers: Deep familiarity with ClickHouse mutation analysis and column handling for ephemeral/materialized columns is required.
71793.problem_summary: Executing a lightweight DELETE on a table containing a MATERIALIZED column that depends on an EPHEMERAL column fails with an UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER error ('Missing columns: <ephemeral_col>'), even when the DELETE WHERE condition does not reference either column.
71793.root_cause_hypothesis: During lightweight DELETE planning or mutation expression construction, ClickHouse attempts to calculate or validate expressions for all default/materialized columns or collects required columns for mutation actions without filtering out materialized columns that do not need to be updated during lightweight delete. Because lightweight delete only writes row masks (_row_exists) or recalculates specific mutation targets, evaluating expressions depending on non-stored EPHEMERAL columns fails when those columns are absent in the storage/reading pipeline.
71793.suggested_approach: Identify the pipeline setup for lightweight DELETE (and mutations handling row masks) and ensure that MATERIALIZED column expressions depending on EPHEMERAL columns are not evaluated or added to required columns when performing operations that do not modify or recompute those MATERIALIZED columns.
prerequisites: Working ClickHouse development environment with C++20 and CMake build toolchain.
Ability to run stateless functional tests (e.g., using ./runner or clickhouse-test).
implementation_steps: Reproduce the issue locally using clickhouse-client or a stateless test with a MergeTree table having a MATERIALIZED column depending on an EPHEMERAL column, followed by a DELETE statement.
Trace the execution stack in InterpreterDeleteQuery and MutationsInterpreter (specifically when preparing the mutation steps and analyzing required columns).

Inspect where expressions for MATERIALIZED columns are gathered (e.g., in MutationsInterpreter or MergeTreeData::getExpressionsForDelayedDefaults / getColumnsForUpdate) and verify whether lightweight delete mistakenly includes re-materialization of columns that are not part of the update.

Adjust the column requirement resolution or mutation DAG builder so that MATERIALIZED columns (and transitively their referenced EPHEMERAL dependencies) are excluded from the required source columns for lightweight DELETE operations.
Verify that regular `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE/MATERIALIZE COLUMN` statements referencing EPHEMERAL columns still handle errors or re-evaluations appropriately.
Add a functional stateless test case under tests/queries/0_stateless/ covering DELETE on tables with MATERIALIZED columns dependent on EPHEMERAL columns.

11942.title: allow_ddl option is not consistent over restarts
11942.feasibility_reason: The issue involves configuration reloading and persistence for profiles (likely ClickHouse users/profiles configuration handling), which might span server startup initialization logic versus runtime configuration updates. A capable developer could trace where `allow_ddl` is initialized and reloaded, but it touches core server startup subsystems.
11942.problem_summary: Setting allow_ddl to 0 in the default profile causes DDL queries (especially ON CLUSTER queries or server-side DDL execution) to fail across all profiles after a server restart, even if an explicit profile has allow_ddl set to 1.
11942.root_cause_hypothesis: The global/system context and internal background execution threads (such as DDLWorker executing ON CLUSTER queries or server initialization tasks) inherit settings from the default profile specified in config.xml (<default_profile>default</default_profile>). When allow_ddl is 0 in the default profile, internal DDL tasks executed by system background threads run with allow_ddl = 0 and fail.
11942.suggested_approach: Ensure that system contexts and internal background workers (specifically DDLWorker and internal cluster task execution) explicitly enforce or bypass `allow_ddl` checks (e.g., setting allow_ddl = 1 or using a privileged internal context) so that restricting user-facing default profiles does not break internal DDL processing across server restarts.
prerequisites: A local ClickHouse build environment with CMake, Ninja, and a C++20 compiler.
A functional ZooKeeper/Keeper cluster configuration to test distributed DDL (ON CLUSTER).
implementation_steps: Reproduce the issue by starting ClickHouse with default profile having `<allow_ddl>0</allow_ddl>` and a custom profile having `<allow_ddl>1</allow_ddl>`, executing a DDL query (particularly with `ON CLUSTER`), and restarting the server.
Inspect `DDLWorker` context initialization to determine what profile or settings are inherited when creating query contexts for executing distributed DDL tasks.
Modify `DDLWorker::processTask` or the context creation logic for internal/distributed query execution to explicitly enable `allow_ddl = 1` in the query context used for executing cluster tasks.
Verify whether any other internal server startup procedures or system queries incorrectly depend on the default profile's `allow_ddl` setting.

Write an integration/functional test verifying that DDL operations (including `ON CLUSTER`) succeed under a privileged profile when the default profile has `allow_ddl = 0` both before and after server restarts.
